title: The Lost Colony of Roanoke: What Really Happened?
title_candidates: The Lost Colony of Roanoke: What Really Happened?
The Lost Colony of Roanoke, Explained (CROATOAN)
What Really Happened to Roanoke's Lost Colonists?
blurb: What really happened to the lost colony of Roanoke? In 1590 John White came back to find 115 settlers gone and CROATOAN carved on a post. Meatball checks the four big theories against the evidence: lost at sea, killed, moved inland (Site X and the hidden fort on White's map), and Croatoan (Hatteras). Sources are in the description.

sources: Roanoke Colony (1587): ~115 settlers under governor John White; Virginia Dare born 18 Aug 1587; White left for England late 1587, delayed by the Anglo-Spanish War and the Armada (1588), returned Aug 1590 to find the settlement abandoned, houses dismantled, palisade standing, 'CROATOAN' carved on a post and 'CRO' on a tree, no Maltese cross (the agreed distress sign); storms stopped him reaching Croatoan — NPS Fort Raleigh National Historic Site, 'The Lost Colony' https://www.nps.gov/fora/learn/historyculture/the-lost-colony.htm ; Wikipedia, Roanoke Colony
Powhatan story: William Strachey (c. 1612) reported Powhatan's claim to have killed settlers; second-hand, no archaeological confirmation — Wikipedia, Roanoke Colony § Investigations and theories

Site X: 2012 British Museum examination of White's map 'La Virginea Pars' found a fort symbol under a patch at the head of the Chowan and Roanoke rivers; First Colony Foundation excavations found 16th-century English-style pottery (Border ware); dating and trade questions remain — First Colony Foundation https://www.firstcolonyfoundation.org ; Wikipedia, Roanoke Colony

Croatoan/Hatteras: Manteo was Croatoan; Croatoan Archaeological Project (Mark Horton, University of Bristol, with Croatoan Archaeological Society) reported 16th-century English objects incl. a rapier hilt, gun parts and a slate on Hatteras; disputed as possible trade goods. John Lawson, A New Voyage to Carolina (1709): Hatteras people said some ancestors were white and 'could talk in a book', some had grey eyes — Wikipedia, Roanoke Colony; John Lawson (1709)

beats.say: In fifteen ninety, a man came home to his family's village and found it empty. A hundred people, gone. One word carved into a post.

beats.say: First, what actually happened. Fifteen eighty-seven. A hundred and fifteen English settlers land on Roanoke Island, off what's now North Carolina.

shots.photo: Roanoke Island, detail of de Bry's map
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry - Roanoke Island detail.jpg
wm:Roanoke map 1584.JPG

beats.say: This was England's second try. The first group, two years earlier, ran out of food, fought with the local people, and went home.

shots.photo: Roanoke Island, detail of de Bry's map
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry - Roanoke Island detail.jpg

beats.say: Men, women and children. Their governor is an artist named John White. A month after landing, his daughter has a baby girl, Virginia Dare, the first English child born in the Americas.

shots.photo: The town of Secotan, after John White (de Bry engraving)
shots.obs: wm:Secoton01.jpg

shots.photo: The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia, Theodor de Bry (1590)
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry 1585 1586.jpg

beats.say: They're short on food. So White sails back to England for supplies. He expects to be gone a few months.
Here's the twist. England goes to war with Spain. The Spanish Armada is coming, and every good ship is kept home. White is stuck for three years.

shots.obs: wm:Elizabeth I (Armada Portrait).jpg

beats.say: He did try once. In fifteen eighty-eight, two small ships left with supplies. French raiders robbed them at sea, and they limped home.
When he finally gets back, it's his granddaughter's third birthday. The houses are gone. The fence is still standing. On a post: Croatoan. On a tree: C R O.

shots.obs: wm:Fort Raleigh National Historic Site earthworks - Sarah Stierch.jpg
wm:Roanoke Colonists Croatoan image from page 146 of Stories of the three Americas. Their discovery and settlement (1890).jpg

beats.say: They had agreed on a signal. If they left in danger, carve a cross. There was no cross.

shots.obs: wm:Roanoke Colonists Croatoan image from page 146 of Stories of the three Americas. Their discovery and settlement (1890).jpg

beats.say: White tried to sail to Croatoan, the island down the coast. A storm drove his ships off. He never came back. So, theory number four.

shots.obs: wm:Cape hatteras 1989.jpg

beats.say: Number four. They tried to sail home and drowned. They did have a small boat, and the Atlantic sinks small boats.
But a hundred people do not fit in one small boat. And the sign on the post doesn't say England. It says Croatoan.

shots.obs: wm:Roanoke Colonists Croatoan image from page 146 of Stories of the three Americas. Their discovery and settlement (1890).jpg

beats.say: I also wouldn't cross an ocean in a rowboat. I float for about four seconds.
Also, they had time. Taking a whole village apart takes weeks. People who are drowning don't plan that far ahead.

shots.obs: wm:Fort Raleigh National Historic Site earthworks - Sarah Stierch.jpg

beats.say: Verdict on number four: unlikely. Number three is darker.

shots.photo: The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia, Theodor de Bry (1590)
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry 1585 1586.jpg

beats.say: Number three. They were killed. Twenty years later, the Jamestown colonists heard a story that the powerful Powhatan chief had wiped out English settlers.

shots.obs: wm:Village of Secotan) - T.B LCCN2001695723.jpg

shots.photo: The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia, Theodor de Bry (1590)
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry 1585 1586.jpg

beats.say: To be fair, the English hadn't been great neighbors. On the first trip, they burned a whole village over one missing silver cup.

shots.photo: The town of Secotan, after John White (de Bry engraving)
shots.obs: wm:Secoton01.jpg

beats.say: So some local people had every reason to be angry. But angry isn't evidence.

shots.obs: wm:Village of Secotan) - T.B LCCN2001695723.jpg

beats.say: Here's the catch. That story is second-hand, written down years later, and nobody ever found the evidence. No battle site. No mass grave.

shots.photo: The town of Secotan, after John White (de Bry engraving)
shots.obs: wm:Secoton01.jpg

beats.say: And the colonists took their houses apart before they left. People under attack don't pack up the furniture.

shots.obs: wm:Fort Raleigh National Historic Site earthworks - Sarah Stierch.jpg

beats.say: Verdict: possible for some of them, not proven. Still to come: a secret drawn on a map, hidden for four hundred years.

beats.say: Number two. They moved inland. In twenty twelve, researchers at the British Museum looked at John White's own map, and found a patch.

shots.photo: The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia, Theodor de Bry (1590)
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry 1585 1586.jpg

shots.photo: Roanoke Island, detail of de Bry's map
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry - Roanoke Island detail.jpg

beats.say: Under the patch, drawn in invisible-ish ink, a symbol for a fort, fifty miles inland at the head of a river.

shots.photo: Roanoke Island, detail of de Bry's map
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry - Roanoke Island detail.jpg

beats.say: Nobody knows why it's covered. One guess: White hid it on purpose, so Spanish spies couldn't read where his people were.

shots.photo: The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia, Theodor de Bry (1590)
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry 1585 1586.jpg

beats.say: Archaeologists dug there. They found English pottery from the right era. They call it Site X, which is the coolest name a field has ever had.

shots.obs: wm:Roanoke map 1584.JPG
wm:Fort Raleigh National Historic Site earthworks - Sarah Stierch.jpg

beats.say: Why go inland at all? The colonists had talked about moving fifty miles into the mainland before White left. He wrote it down.

shots.photo: Roanoke Island, detail of de Bry's map
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry - Roanoke Island detail.jpg

beats.say: But pottery can be traded, and the dates aren't tight. Verdict: promising, not proven. And number one has something Site X doesn't. A matching word.

shots.photo: The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia, Theodor de Bry (1590)
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry 1585 1586.jpg

beats.say: Number one. They did exactly what the post said. They went to Croatoan, the island we now call Hatteras, home of the Croatoan people, who were friendly to the English.

shots.obs: wm:Cape hatteras 1989.jpg
wm:Roanoke Colonists Croatoan image from page 146 of Stories of the three Americas. Their discovery and settlement (1890).jpg

beats.say: One of the colony's own men, Manteo, was a Croatoan. His family lived there. If you're hungry and stranded, you go where you have friends.

shots.photo: The town of Secotan, after John White (de Bry engraving)
shots.obs: wm:Secoton01.jpg

beats.say: Manteo had even been to England, twice. He was the colony's translator. The English baptised him the summer they landed.

shots.obs: wm:Elizabeth I (Armada Portrait).jpg

beats.say: Here's the evidence. Digs on Hatteras have turned up English things from the right century. Pieces of a sword. Parts of guns. A writing slate.

shots.obs: wm:Cape hatteras 1989.jpg
wm:Fort Raleigh National Historic Site earthworks - Sarah Stierch.jpg

beats.say: In nineteen ninety-eight, a ring with a lion on it turned up there too. It was first called a gold, Elizabethan ring. Later tests said brass, and the argument continues.

shots.obs: wm:Cape hatteras 1989.jpg

beats.say: And a century later, an English explorer wrote that some Hatteras people said their ancestors could read in a book, and some had grey eyes.

shots.obs: wm:Village of Secotan) - T.B LCCN2001695723.jpg

beats.say: Here's the honest part. The objects could have been traded, and there's no grave, no name, no smoking gun. Archaeologists still argue.

shots.obs: wm:Cape hatteras 1989.jpg

beats.say: I'd also move in with the neighbors. As long as they're not hungry. You know why.

shots.photo: The town of Secotan, after John White (de Bry engraving)
shots.obs: wm:Secoton01.jpg

beats.say: Verdict: the colony probably split up and joined the people around them, mostly at Croatoan. But nobody has proved it. Unsolved.

shots.obs: wm:Roanoke Colonists Croatoan image from page 146 of Stories of the three Americas. Their discovery and settlement (1890).jpg

beats.say: So, what really happened to the lost colony? Most likely, it wasn't lost at all. It just stopped being English, and nobody wrote it down.

shots.photo: The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia, Theodor de Bry (1590)
shots.obs: wm:The Carte of all the Coast of Virginia by Theodor de Bry 1585 1586.jpg

shots.photo: The town of Secotan, after John White (de Bry engraving)
shots.obs: wm:Secoton01.jpg

beats.say: Some families on the Outer Banks believe they descend from the colonists. DNA studies have tried to check, and so far nothing is settled.

shots.obs: wm:Cape hatteras 1989.jpg

beats.say: The spooky version is a vanished town and a cursed word. The real version is people surviving, and leaving a note saying where they went.

shots.obs: wm:Roanoke Colonists Croatoan image from page 146 of Stories of the three Americas. Their discovery and settlement (1890).jpg

beats.say: So, were you right? Where did they go? Tell me in the comments.
